explanations.explanation: Spot on, baker! When food runs short in Bethlehem, Elimelech packs up his family and heads east into the country of Moab (Ruth 1:1). It was a big journey across the river into foreign territory just to find bread. That move set their whole story in motion.

Egypt is where folks like Abraham and Jacob went during hard famines, but this family heads somewhere else. Ruth 1:1 says they went to live in the land of Moab. It was across the Jordan, right next door to Judah.
Edom is down south, but this family did not go there. Ruth 1:1 tells us they crossed over to reside in the land of Moab. That is where Elimelech took his wife and his two boys to escape the hunger.
You nailed it, friend! Mahlon and Chilion marry local Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth (Ruth 1:4). Ruth enters the family right here, and her devotion is about to shine brighter than fresh tin pans.

Rachel was Jacob's wife back in Genesis, way before this family ever packed their bags. Ruth 1:4 tells us the two Moabite wives were named Orpah and Ruth. That second daughter-in-law is the very one this book is named after!
Dinah was Jacob's daughter back in the older stories of Genesis. In Ruth 1:4, the two women who married Naomi's sons are named Orpah and Ruth. Keep an eye on Ruth, because she is not going anywhere.

That is the sad truth, baker. Naomi had already lost her husband, and then both Mahlon and Chilion pass away in Moab (Ruth 1:5). She is left completely alone without her boys or her husband in a foreign country. A heavy blow for anyone to carry.

explanations.answer: Her house in Moab burns down
explanations.explanation: Losing a house would be rough, but Naomi faces something far more heartbreaking. Ruth 1:5 tells us both of her sons, Mahlon and Chilion, died. After losing her husband earlier, she is left without any of her men.

explanations.answer: She falls sick and loses her sight
explanations.explanation: The text does not mention any sickness or blindness hitting Naomi. The heartbreak here is deep grief, because Ruth 1:5 says both Mahlon and Chilion died. Naomi was left completely alone without her husband and without her two boys.

That is it, friend! Word travels across the border that the LORD visited His people and brought bread back to Bethlehem (Ruth 1:6). Hearing there is food again gives Naomi a reason to pack up and head back to her hometown.

Israel did not have an earthly king yet in those days, since the judges were still ruling. What Naomi heard was much simpler and met their immediate need: the LORD had provided His people with food (Ruth 1:6).

There were plenty of battles back in the time of the judges, but that is not the news Naomi got. Ruth 1:6 says she heard the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food. Bread was back on the table in Judah!

explanations.answer: Go back to their mothers' homes
explanations.explanation: Right on the money! Naomi cares about these young women and knows life as a foreign widow in Judah would be hard, so she tells each to return to her mother's house (Ruth 1:8). She wanted them to have a real chance at a future.

explanations.answer: Walk faster to beat the dark
explanations.explanation: Traveling before nightfall is always smart on dirt roads, but Naomi is thinking about their whole lives, not just sundown. In Ruth 1:8, she tells both daughters-in-law to turn around and go back to their mothers' homes.

explanations.answer: Stay close to her the whole way
explanations.explanation: You might expect a lonely traveler to cling to company, but Naomi does the exact opposite. She puts the young women first and urges them to return to their mothers' homes instead of following her (Ruth 1:8).

True it is! Naomi prays a blessing over both of them: 'May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband' (Ruth 1:9). She genuinely wanted them to be cared for, even if it meant traveling the rest of the road alone.

It actually is true, baker! In Ruth 1:9, Naomi specifically blesses them by asking that the LORD help each of them find rest in the home of a new husband. She was hoping they would remarry and find security back among their own people.

explanations.answer: We will return with you to your people
explanations.explanation: You got it! Through their tears, both Orpah and Ruth refuse to abandon her at first, saying, 'Surely we will return with you to your people' (Ruth 1:10). They loved Naomi enough that they were ready to leave their homeland behind with her.

explanations.answer: We will stay in Moab and wait for you
explanations.explanation: They were not planning on waiting around for a postcard, friend. Right after Naomi kisses them, both women weep out loud and declare they will go with her to her people (Ruth 1:10).

explanations.answer: We will come visit you in Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: This was not a casual vacation promise. Both daughters-in-law were ready for a permanent move, telling Naomi they would return with her to her people in Judah (Ruth 1:10).

explanations.answer: Would you wait for them to grow up
explanations.explanation: Spot on! Naomi is laying out the harsh reality of their culture. Even if she remarried that very night and had baby boys, she asks, 'would you wait for them to grow up?' (Ruth 1:13). She knew that waiting years for infants to become husbands made no practical sense.

explanations.answer: Would you raise them as your own
explanations.explanation: Naomi is talking about future husbands for them under ancient family customs, not asking for babysitters! In Ruth 1:13, she asks if they would actually wait around for infant boys to grow up into grown men to marry them.

explanations.answer: Would you go ahead to Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: She is not sending them ahead as scouts, baker. Naomi is arguing that staying with her has no future, asking if they would really wait around for newborn sons of hers to grow up and marry them (Ruth 1:13).

explanations.answer: The LORD's hand has turned against her
explanations.explanation: Exactly right. Naomi's grief runs deep, and she tells them, 'it is much more bitter for me than for you, because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me' (Ruth 1:13). She feels like heaven itself has struck down her household, leaving her empty-handed.

explanations.answer: The people of Judah have turned against her
explanations.explanation: The people back home had not done anything to her; in fact, she had not even seen them in ten years! Naomi's struggle is with what she feels God has done, saying the hand of the LORD has gone out against her (Ruth 1:13).

explanations.answer: The people of Moab have turned against her
explanations.explanation: The text never says the Moabite neighbors mistreated her. Naomi is looking at all the family tragedy she suffered and concludes that the hand of the LORD had gone out against her personally (Ruth 1:13).

True indeed! After hearing Naomi's practical reasoning, Orpah kisses her mother-in-law goodbye and turns back toward Moab (Ruth 1:14). It was an affectionate, tearful parting, but Orpah chose to take Naomi's advice.
It really is true, friend. Ruth 1:14 says the women wept aloud again, and then Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye. She listened to Naomi and decided to head back home to her family.

Hold your rolling pin, baker, because Ruth does the opposite! Ruth 1:14 says that while Orpah kissed Naomi goodbye, Ruth clung to her. Ruth refused to pack up and walk away, sticking with Naomi no matter what lay ahead.
You got it, baker, that statement is false! While Orpah turns back toward her homeland, Ruth 1:14 tells us that Ruth clung right to Naomi. She was not leaving her mother-in-law's side for anything.

True it is! Naomi points down the dusty road and tells Ruth, 'your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods; follow her back home' (Ruth 1:15). Even with only Ruth left beside her, Naomi tests her resolve and gives her an exit.

It actually is true, friend! In Ruth 1:15, Naomi really does tell Ruth to turn around and follow Orpah back to her people and her gods. She wanted Ruth to count the full cost of staying with a penniless widow.

explanations.answer: Naomi's God will be her God
explanations.explanation: Box-worthy answer, baker! Ruth makes one of the boldest declarations in all of Scripture: 'your people will be my people, and your God will be my God' (Ruth 1:16). She is leaving Moab's false gods behind and tying her life completely to the LORD.

explanations.answer: She will take care of Naomi's house
explanations.explanation: Cleaning the house is fine work, but Ruth goes infinitely deeper than household chores. In Ruth 1:16, she commits her whole soul, telling Naomi that her people will be Ruth's people, and Naomi's God will be her God.

explanations.answer: She will learn all the ways of Judah
explanations.explanation: She certainly had to adapt to life in Judah later on, but Ruth 1:16 records something much more profound. Ruth promises that Naomi's people will be her people, and Naomi's God will be her God. That was a total commitment of faith.

That is the word, baker! Ruth seals her promise with a solemn oath, asking the LORD to punish her severely if anything but death separates them (Ruth 1:17). She was in this walk for life, right down to the grave.

Distance could not keep these two apart! Ruth says in Ruth 1:17 that she will go wherever Naomi goes, swearing that nothing short of death will separate them. She was glued to Naomi all the way to Bethlehem.

Naomi had just spent verses urging them to remarry, but Ruth is not letting marriage get in the way of her loyalty. In Ruth 1:17, Ruth declares that only death itself will ever separate her from Naomi.

explanations.answer: She stops trying to persuade her
explanations.explanation: You got it! When Naomi sees that jaw set and realizes Ruth is absolutely determined to stay with her, she stops trying to talk her out of it (Ruth 1:18). There was no turning Ruth around after a speech like that.

explanations.answer: She sends her back after Orpah
explanations.explanation: Naomi already tried pointing after Orpah once, but after Ruth's oath, that argument was over. Ruth 1:18 says that when Naomi saw Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped trying to persuade her.

explanations.answer: She tells her to wait in Moab
explanations.explanation: They were already standing out on the road together, well on their way. Ruth 1:18 tells us that seeing Ruth's fierce determination made Naomi finally drop the debate and let Ruth walk beside her.

Spot on! When the pair walks through the gates, the whole town buzzes with excitement, and the local women exclaim, 'Can this be Naomi?' (Ruth 1:19). Ten years of hardship and grief had clearly taken a visible toll on her.

They did not ask about Elimelech right at the gate, though the sad answer would soon be clear to everyone. The women of Bethlehem look at her weathered face and exclaim, 'Can this be Naomi?' (Ruth 1:19).

Ruth was certainly a stranger from Moab, but all eyes first lock onto the woman they used to know. The women of the town are stunned by how much Naomi has changed, asking, 'Can this be Naomi?' (Ruth 1:19).

Fine work, baker! Naomi means 'pleasant,' but she says, 'Do not call me Naomi... Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me' (Ruth 1:20). 'Mara' means bitter, and it matched the ache in her heart.

Hannah is another godly woman who experienced deep grief in 1 Samuel, but that is not what Naomi chooses. In Ruth 1:20, she tells the townspeople to call her Mara, a name connected to bitterness, because of how hard life had been.
Leah was one of the matriarchs back in Genesis. Here in Ruth 1:20, Naomi asks to be called Mara. She felt like pleasantness was gone, and only bitter sorrow remained from her years away.

Careful on that flip, baker! Naomi actually says the exact reverse: 'I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty' (Ruth 1:21). She left Bethlehem with a husband and two sons, and she walked back in with empty hands.

You nailed it, that statement is false! In Ruth 1:21, Naomi laments, 'I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty.' She looked back on leaving with a whole family and felt like she had returned with nothing left.

That is the crop, friend! Ruth and Naomi arrive in Bethlehem right at the beginning of the barley harvest (Ruth 1:22). After years of famine and barren grief, fresh grain is finally being gathered in the fields. A little hint of hope on the horizon!

Wheat harvest came a little later in the season. Ruth 1:22 specifically tells us they stepped into Bethlehem right at the beginning of the barley harvest. The sickles were just starting to swing in the barley fields.

Olive harvest happens in the autumn, long after the springtime grain is cut. According to Ruth 1:22, the two women arrive in town right as the barley harvest was kicking off. Bethlehem, the house of bread, was finally full of grain again.
